title: Pull Request Quality Gates
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of pull request quality gates and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to pull request quality gates.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on pull request quality gates. Required status checks and branch rules prevent a merge until the intended validation has passed; reviewers should verify expected checks cannot be skipped. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Pull Request Quality Gates matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Required status checks and branch rules prevent a merge until the intended validation has passed; reviewers should verify expected checks cannot be skipped. A useful CI pipeline gives a clear pass/fail result for relevant quality checks. Keep fast checks early, use services only when tests need them, and ensure required checks cannot be skipped accidentally.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Required status checks and branch rules prevent a merge until the intended validation has passed; reviewers should verify expected checks cannot be skipped. A useful CI pipeline gives a clear pass/fail result for relevant quality checks. Keep fast checks early, use services only when tests need them, and ensure required checks cannot be skipped accidentally. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Required status checks
items.text: Make the check deterministic and fail with a meaningful status when requirements are not met. Preserve reports where useful and configure required branch checks to match the checks the workflow actually emits.

items.title: Branch protection and rulesets
items.text: Use filters to reduce unnecessary runs only when skipped work is genuinely unrelated. Include shared dependencies and test the changed and unchanged path cases so required checks are not bypassed.

items.title: Preventing merges when checks fail
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Naming stable status checks
items.text: Make the check deterministic and fail with a meaningful status when requirements are not met. Preserve reports where useful and configure required branch checks to match the checks the workflow actually emits.

items.title: Reviewing skipped or missing checks
items.text: For reviewing skipped or missing checks, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Balancing required checks with workflow efficiency
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

content_blocks.code:
name: Required pull request checks
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  checks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "Run lint, tests, and build checks"
content_blocks.expected_output: A pull request targeting `main` receives a single checks status; configure branch rules separately to require this exact status.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Confirm the stable status-check name and branch-rule configuration in a test repository.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Do not assume the workflow alone enforces merge protection.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to pull request quality gates. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain pull request quality gates, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Build CI checks that produce repeatable evidence and protect merge quality.

content.task: Apply pull request quality gates to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Required status checks and branch rules prevent a merge until the intended validation has passed; reviewers should verify expected checks cannot be skipped.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Required status checks and branch rules prevent a merge until the intended validation has passed; reviewers should verify expected checks cannot be skipped. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Required status checks and branch rules prevent a merge until the intended validation has passed; reviewers should verify expected checks cannot be skipped.

A useful CI pipeline gives a clear pass/fail result for relevant quality checks. Keep fast checks early, use services only when tests need them, and ensure required checks cannot be skipped accidentally.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
